doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

chapter: New York, the clarinet and first gigs
title: Practicing with his sister, high school band, first paid gig
summary: His sister's teasing spurred practice; he played in high school band and mentions his first paid gig in Trenton.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: List was a very good teacher. But I went home and I had a clarinet, it costs 25 bucks. And we paid it off a dollar a week or two dollars a week or something like that. And I wasn’t an instant success with it because I went home and I was going to master this sucker you know. And I had a younger sister —I had, she’s passed on — and she was musical, she danced. She did Hungarian folk dancing, really good. And as a matter of fact her teacher was this old lady, it was Mrs. Serly, and her son was Tibor Serly, who finished the Bartok whatever it is, you know, there was a guy, Tibor Serly finished I think the Bartok Concerto or something. When Bartok died before it was finished he finished it. And he used to play piano for their dancing. Remember him, I said, you know who that was? Well anyway, where was I?
How did you make your first dollar with your clarinet?

Oh, oh, oh. Well this is very deep. So anyhow, well let me finish the story about my sister. So I went home with the clarinet and I started to practice and she laughed and said “you sound like a duck,” which led me to practice. And I evidently improved very quickly. I mean I just ate it up. So then I ended up in high school and I played in the high school band. And I never got into athletics much, you know, football. “You’d make a good football player” you know. I wanted to play the clarinet. So my first dollar with the clarinet, would you believe, was a gig in Trenton, New Jersey and the bass player was Pops Foster. It was a bowling alley in Trenton, New Jersey. I think it paid a lot of money, like 35 bucks or something, which was a lot of money.
